title: Weekly gemcitabine with radiotherapy
indication_text: Bladder cancer treated with concurrent gemcitabine and radiotherapy.
purpose: Help radiotherapy treat bladder cancer as part of a selected bladder-preservation plan.
schedule_summary: Gemcitabine 100 mg/m² is given weekly on days 1, 8, 15 and 22, two to four hours before radiotherapy. There are four planned gemcitabine doses in one course. This low-dose schedule is different from gemcitabine 1000 mg/m² chemotherapy.
administration_text: Gemcitabine is given through a vein over 30 minutes. The chemotherapy and radiotherapy teams coordinate the same-day appointments so radiotherapy follows two to four hours later.
monitoring_summary: Full blood count weekly; kidney and liver tests at the end of the course as specified in the regimen, with extra testing if clinically required. Review bowel, urinary, skin, breathing and general symptoms during treatment.
safety_note: Follow your own prescription and hospital instructions. This information supports a discussion; it does not authorise treatment.
urgent_extra: Call oncology immediately for fever, shaking chills, suddenly feeling unwell, unusual bleeding, new breathlessness, very little urine, severe rash or vomiting that prevents drinking. Follow your hospital’s temperature and contact instructions. Severe breathing difficulty, chest pain, collapse or seizures: call 112/999.

phases_note: NCCP 00759 is four weekly 100 mg/m² gemcitabine doses with radiotherapy. Do not import a 1000 mg/m² gemcitabine dose, repeated chemotherapy cycles or another radiotherapy prescription.

agents.name: Gemcitabine
agents.explanation: Gemcitabine interferes with making DNA, which dividing cancer cells need. Healthy blood-forming cells and other tissues can also be affected.
agents.watch: Report fever, unusual bleeding, breathlessness, rash, swelling or reduced urine promptly.
risks: Low blood counts, serious infection, anaemia and bleeding
Nausea, vomiting, fatigue, flu-like symptoms and swelling
Rash, sore mouth and liver-test changes
Uncommon or rare serious lung inflammation, kidney injury including haemolytic uraemic syndrome, severe skin reactions and capillary leak

anatomy: New cough or breathlessness needs urgent assessment.
Report soreness or ulcers that interfere with drinking.
Blood tests check the liver; report yellow eyes or dark urine.
Report frequent diarrhoea, abdominal pain or inability to drink.
Report burning, blood in urine, reduced urine or inability to pass urine.
Fever, sudden illness or unusual bleeding needs urgent advice.
Follow the skin-care plan; report blistering or widespread rash urgently.
Fatigue can build during treatment. Call if suddenly weak or unwell.

evidence.title: GemX · phase II study
evidence.summary: GemX was a single-arm phase II study of 50 people with muscle-invasive bladder cancer. Forty-four patients, 88% of the study group, had a complete response at the bladder examination after treatment.
evidence.intro: GemX was a single-arm phase II study of 50 people with muscle-invasive bladder cancer. Forty-four patients, 88% of the study group, had a complete response at the bladder examination after treatment.
evidence.caveat: A complete endoscopic response is not proof of cure. This small study had no randomised comparison with surgery or other chemoradiation, so its result cannot establish which option is best for an individual.
evidence.interpretation: A complete endoscopic response is not proof of cure. This small study had no randomised comparison with surgery or other chemoradiation, so its result cannot establish which option is best for an individual.

questions.q: What is the treatment trying to do?
questions.a: Help radiotherapy treat bladder cancer as part of a selected bladder-preservation plan. Radiotherapy is the local cancer treatment; gemcitabine helps sensitise cancer cells to it. Radiation dose, fractions and any interruptions are agreed by radiation oncology. Regular bladder surveillance is still needed; surgery may be considered for persistent or returning cancer.

Gemcitabine 100 mg/m² is given weekly on days 1, 8, 15 and 22, two to four hours before radiotherapy. There are four planned gemcitabine doses in one course. This low-dose schedule is different from gemcitabine 1000 mg/m² chemotherapy.

questions.q: Does a delay mean treatment has failed?
questions.a: No. Blood counts, organ function and symptoms can make a delay or dose change safer. Your team decides whether and when to give the next dose.

questions.q: Who do I contact if unwell?
questions.a: Use your verified oncology daytime or out-of-hours number. If you cannot reach the team, seek urgent medical assessment. Severe symptoms require 112/999.
